what_its_for: Isoniazid is an antibiotic used to treat or prevent tuberculosis (TB), a serious infection that mainly affects the lungs. Your doctor may prescribe it to treat active TB disease or to prevent TB if you have been exposed to it (this is called latent TB).
how_to_take: Take isoniazid exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet or liquid by mouth. It is best to take it on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, so your body absorbs it better. If it upsets your stomach, you may take it with a small amount of food. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not skip doses or stop taking it early, even if you feel better. TB requires a full course of treatment, which may last 6 to 9 months or longer.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the reason you are taking it. A common adult dose for treating active TB is 5 mg per kilogram of body weight once daily (usually 300 mg per day). For preventing TB, the typical adult dose is also 300 mg once daily. Children's doses are based on their weight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss doses often, talk to your doctor or pharmacist for help.
storage: Store isoniazid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking isoniazid because it greatly increases the risk of serious liver damage. Avoid foods high in tyramine or histamine, such as aged cheeses, cured meats, sauerkraut, soy sauce, and some fish like tuna and skipjack, as they can cause a dangerous reaction (flushing, headache, fast heartbeat). Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take because isoniazid can interact with many drugs, including antacids containing aluminum (take them at least 1 hour after isoniazid), seizure medications, and certain diabetes medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice any of these warning signs: yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or unusual tiredness — these may be signs of liver problems. Also call your doctor if you develop numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet (nerve problems); vision changes; mood changes or confusion; skin rash or itching; or fever. Liver problems from isoniazid can be serious and even life-threatening if not caught early.
when_it_works: For latent TB (prevention), isoniazid works quietly in the background to kill the dormant TB bacteria, and you likely will not feel any different. For active TB, you may start to feel better within a few weeks, but it is very important to finish the entire course of treatment. The bacteria can come back stronger (resistant) if you stop early. Full treatment usually takes at least 6 months.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Isoniazid can be used during pregnancy when needed, as untreated TB poses greater risk to the mother and baby. Talk to your doctor about the benefits and risks. Breastfeeding: Small amounts pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor, but breastfeeding is generally considered safe. Older adults: Older adults are at higher risk of liver problems and should have regular liver function tests while on this medication. Kidney or liver disease: Dose adjustments or extra monitoring may be needed. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): Doctors often recommend taking vitamin B6 (25 to 50 mg daily) alongside isoniazid, especially if you are pregnant, have diabetes, drink alcohol, or have nerve problems, to reduce the risk of nerve side effects.
